extracted.intended_audience: humor researchers, linguists, comedy writers, and students of verbal-humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH) to analyze, compare, or compose verbal jokes by specifying six hierarchical Knowledge Resources (SO, LM, SI, TA, NS, LA). Useful for describing joke similarity and diagnosing joke effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Opposition (SO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pair of opposed scripts identified by SSTH (real/unreal, sex/non-sex, etc.). The deepest invariant of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic question: which two opposed scripts are at play? Notes: SO is the deepest layer and must be a valid script opposition (necessary condition #1). Two jokes that share only SO are perceived as the same kind of joke (low surface similarity). Examples in SSTH: real vs. unreal, sex vs. non-sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The resolution device — the (often fallacious) reasoning that makes the script switch feel justifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attardo's examples: Juxtaposition (placing two scripts side by side); Figure–ground reversal; Faulty reasoning / fallacy; Cratylism (sound–meaning iconicity); Garden path (audience led to wrong inference, then corrected); Self‑undermining (statement undercuts its own premise); Almost‑situation / parallelism / chiasmus / reasoning from false premises; Vacuous reversal / role exchange / coincidence / analogy. Diagnostic question: what reasoning device justifies the switch? Notes: LM must be discoverable (necessary condition #2); often the place to locate the joke's mechanism when analyzing or reformulating a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The props, setting, participants, and activities anchoring the joke (e.g., doctor's office, bar, desert island).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic question: what setting/props/activities anchor the joke? Notes: SI must be apt to support both scripts (necessary condition #3). Two jokes can share SI but differ in SO; SI contributes to perceived similarity but is lower in the hierarchy than SO/LM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The butt of the joke — who or what is being mocked (ethnic group, profession, character type). Some jokes have no TA (i.e., are non‑targeted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic question: who or what is being mocked, if anyone? Notes: Presence/selection of TA must be calibrated to the audience (necessary condition #4). Some successful jokes are explicitly non‑targeted (resolution-only humor). Ethical/audience considerations are relevant when choosing TA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre or rhetorical form used to deliver the joke (e.g., simple narrative, dialogue/question–answer, riddle, pseudo‑riddle, aside/parenthetical, garden‑path narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic question: what genre or rhetorical form is this (riddle, narrative, dialogue, etc.)? Notes: NS should be appropriate to delivery context (necessary condition #5). Changing NS can produce variants of the same joke by altering surface realization while retaining deeper KRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (LA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface verbal realization: exact word selection, phrasing, syntax, and the specific linguistic realization of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic question: are word choices and ordering optimized for the punch? Notes: Language choices should maximize surprise — placing the punchline at the end, ordering key words for cognitive effect (necessary condition #6). Two jokes that share LA are nearly identical; LA is the most surface, lowest-level KR and is where timing, wording, and micro‑stylistic devices operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy / Joke similarity prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The six Knowledge Resources are hierarchically ordered (SO highest/most abstract → LA lowest/most surface); sharing higher-level KRs yields greater perceived similarity between jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from the model: jokes that share LA are nearly identical; jokes that share only SO are merely the same kind of joke. The hierarchy matters for comparing and classifying jokes: higher KR commonality predicts greater similarity and interchangeability; lower-KR commonality yields more surface variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary conditions for a successful verbal joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful verbal joke requires: (1) a valid Script Opposition; (2) a discoverable Logical Mechanism; (3) an apt Situation that supports both scripts; (4) a Target (or none for non‑targeted jokes) calibrated to audience; (5) an appropriate Narrative Strategy for delivery; (6) Language choices that maximize surprise (punchline placement, key-word ordering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as a diagnostic checklist when evaluating or composing jokes. Pay particular attention to audience calibration for TA and to final wording/timing for LA. The list synthesizes the six KRs into prescriptive conditions for joke construction and evaluation.
